prompt.context: Our client is a large international airline based in a major hub airport. For the last few years, our client has sold its spare maintenance capacity to other airlines in an ad hoc way. Our client's CEO wants to review this behavior in a strategic way and make a strategic decision about whether and how to continue.
prompt.question: How should the client approach the strategic decision about its maintenance in-sourcing activities? What would you recommend?

clarifying_info.q: What type of maintenance are we talking about?
clarifying_info.a: The client is focused on between-flight maintenance, not less frequent overhaul maintenance, which the CEO feels is beyond the firm's scope.

clarifying_info.q: What are the units on the profit axis in Exhibit 1?
clarifying_info.a: Revenue is in billions of dollars; profit is a percent of revenue — the graph is intentionally ambiguous, so you should ask for clarification.

clarifying_info.q: What are the units on the axes in Exhibit 2?
clarifying_info.a: Revenue is in millions of dollars; profit is a percent of revenue — same dual-axis ambiguity as Exhibit 1.

clarifying_info.q: What share of maintenance revenue/profit comes from external (in-sourced) customers?
clarifying_info.a: 50% of the Maintenance division's revenue and profit comes from in-house (internal) use; the other 50% comes from selling to outside airlines.

exhibits.title: Airline's Divisions — Revenue and Profit
exhibits.shows: A dual-axis bar chart comparing the airline's divisions (Maintenance, Passenger, Cargo, Staffing, Private Jets, Re-Supply) on two metrics. One axis runs from 0 to 18 and the other from 0 to 16; units are not labeled on the chart itself.

data.note: Left axis scale 0–18, right axis scale 0–16; revenue and profit series shown as separate bars per division; units deliberately unlabeled

exhibits.title: Maintenance Division Departments — Revenue and Profit
exhibits.shows: A dual-axis bar chart comparing departments within the Maintenance division (Hydraulics, Engine, Avionics, Fuselage, Electrical) on revenue and profit. One axis runs 0–4500 and the other 0–25; units are not labeled on the chart itself.

data.note: Left axis scale 0–4500, right axis scale 0–25; revenue and profit series shown as separate bars per department; units deliberately unlabeled

framework: 1. Demand — (A) Market size and growth; (B) Segments (price sensitivity, usage needs, purchase decisions); (C) Complements/substitutes such as buying new planes

2. Supply — (A) Number of competitors, market share, and changes; (B) Financial benchmarks (revenue, cost, profit and trends); (C) Differentiation (type of service: avionics-only, between-flight check-up, warranties, quality); (D) Barriers to entry (location constraints, skills shortage, limited tarmac real estate)

3. Company — (A) Objective (profit, revenue, market share); (B) Financials (revenue, cost, profit and trends); (C) Maintenance offering and competitive advantage; (D) Maintenance division metrics — is it a profit center, how to balance internal vs. external demand?
4. Options — Halt in-sourcing; No change; Increase in-sourcing; Spin off Maintenance as a separate entity

questions.prompt: How should we evaluate the Maintenance division? (Exhibit 1)
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize the dual-axis graph ambiguity and ask what units each axis represents (revenue in $B, profit in % of revenue). Strong answers note that Maintenance generates the highest or near-highest revenue AND the highest profit margin among all divisions, making it the best-performing unit. Candidate should rule out halting the in-sourcing activity. Bonus: mention that limited tarmac real estate is a barrier to entry for competitors, and distinguish between between-flight check-ups and annual overhauls.

math.setup: Revenue is in billions of dollars; profit is a percent of revenue. Reading Exhibit 1: Maintenance has approximately the highest revenue bar (~16–18 on the revenue scale) and a high profit-margin bar. 50% of Maintenance revenue and profit comes from external in-sourcing.
steps: Identify which axis is revenue ($B) and which is profit (%) by asking the interviewer
Compare Maintenance to other divisions on both dimensions
Observe that Maintenance leads or ties for both revenue and profitability
Note that halting in-sourcing would sacrifice significant external revenue
math.answer: Maintenance is the highest or among the highest revenue-generating and most profitable division; in-sourcing should not be halted.

questions.prompt: How does Exhibit 2 affect your thinking? (Exhibit 2)
questions.guidance: Candidate should again recognize dual-axis ambiguity (revenue in $M, profit in %). Strong answers conclude that Engine and Avionics departments generate high revenue at high margins, while Hydraulics generates lower revenue at a lower margin. The business insight is that additional capital should be allocated to the highest marginal return — Engines and Avionics — and resources should be shifted away from Hydraulics. Bonus: flag that shutting down Hydraulics has strategic implications — it may be a loss-leader or part of an indivisible maintenance package that clients require as a bundle.

math.setup: Revenue is in millions of dollars; profit is a percent of revenue. 50% of each department's revenue and profit comes from in-house use.
steps: Identify units on each axis (ask interviewer: revenue $M left, profit % right)
Compare Engine and Avionics vs. Hydraulics on both revenue and margin
Engine and Avionics: high revenue (approaching 4000–4500 $M range) and high profit margin (~20–25%)
Hydraulics: lower revenue and lower margin relative to Engine/Avionics
Conclude: shift incremental resources from Hydraulics to Engine and Avionics
math.answer: Engine and Avionics are the highest-value departments; Hydraulics is the weakest. Incremental resources should go to Engine and Avionics.

brainstorming.prompt: What strategic options does the client have for its Maintenance division, and what factors would you weigh in evaluating them?

categories.name: Strategic options
ideas: Maintain the status quo (continue ad hoc selling)
Increase and formalize in-sourcing by expanding capacity or marketing to more airlines
Spin off the Maintenance division as a separate standalone business

categories.name: Demand-side factors
ideas: Size and growth of the external airline maintenance market
Segments: between-flight checks vs. overhauls vs. avionics-only
Substitutes: airlines buying new planes instead of maintaining old ones
Airline fleet renewal cycles reducing demand for older-plane maintenance

categories.name: Supply-side factors
ideas: Number and capability of competing maintenance providers
Barriers to entry: limited tarmac space, specialized skills, regulatory certifications
Differentiation: specialized expertise in Engines and Avionics
Plane manufacturer warranty extensions reducing demand for third-party maintenance

categories.name: Company factors
ideas: Opportunity cost of maintenance capacity used internally vs. sold externally
Operational interdependency: Hydraulics may be needed to offer a complete maintenance package
Denying competitors the opportunity to build maintenance scale
Balance between internal demand and external revenue

recommendation: We recommend increasing Maintenance in-sourcing activities, even at the cost of shifting resources from less profitable divisions such as Staffing to Maintenance
Within the Maintenance division, resources should be shifted from Hydraulics to Engines and Avionics, which generate higher revenue and higher profit margins
risks: Airlines updating their fleets with newer aircraft will reduce demand for maintenance services over time
Plane manufacturers increasing their warranties will reduce demand for third-party maintenance
Shutting down or shrinking Hydraulics could break an indivisible maintenance package offering, reducing overall attractiveness to external clients
next_steps: Investigate how to increase revenue and profitability of the client's other divisions (Passenger, Cargo, Staffing, etc.)
Assess whether Hydraulics is a loss-leader required to anchor the full maintenance contract — if so, model the revenue impact of removing it
Quantify the tarmac capacity constraint and evaluate whether capital investment in additional capacity is justified given maintenance margins
